name: C#
summary: Microsoft’s statically typed, object-oriented language for .NET, which made `async` and `await` mainstream and gains a new version every November.
intro: The C# compiler (Roslyn) translates source code into common intermediate language (CIL), a CPU-independent instruction set, plus metadata that describes every type. At run time the .NET just-in-time compiler turns that CIL into native code for the machine, method by method, as it is first called. Memory is managed by the runtime’s garbage collector. Native AOT publishing can instead compile a whole app ahead of time to a self-contained executable, which starts faster but gives up dynamic loading and runtime code generation.

C# began in 2002 as a simple, object-oriented language that looked a lot like Java, and has borrowed widely since: generics in C# 2.0 (2005), LINQ queries and lambdas in 3.0 (2007), and `async`/`await` in C# 5.0 (2012). An `async` method returns a `Task` and can `await` other tasks; while it waits, the thread isn’t blocked and can do other work, and the compiler transforms the method so that it carries on when the task completes. Since 2020 a new version has shipped every November with .NET; C# 14 arrived in November 2025.
The language is standardized as ECMA-334 (first edition December 2001), and the compiler and runtime have been open source since 2014.
strengths: Strong static typing: every variable’s type is known at compile time, so the compiler and editor catch misuse before the program runs
`async`/`await` makes non-blocking code read like ordinary sequential code
LINQ gives one query syntax for in-memory collections, XML or JSON, and databases
Generics are kept by the runtime, so `List<int>` stores plain integers and type arguments are visible to reflection
JIT compilation by default, or Native AOT for faster startup, a smaller memory footprint and no installed runtime
limits: Native AOT apps can’t load assemblies dynamically or generate code at runtime, and need trimming, which some reflection-heavy libraries don’t support
Calling a blocking method such as `Task.Wait()` instead of awaiting blocks the current thread and throws away the benefit of async code

snippet.title: Two awaited calls that wait at the same time (a whole program with top-level statements)
source: await Task.Delay(500);   // stands in for a network call; the thread is free meanwhile
int[] prices = await Task.WhenAll(tea, cake);   // both waits overlap: about 0.5 s in total

story: In the late 1990s Microsoft started internal projects, partly in response to Java, that became the .NET platform and its main language. Anders Hejlsberg, who had written the compiler Borland sold as Turbo Pascal and led the team that designed Delphi, led the C# design team, which met in the same room, three days a week, for years.

Microsoft announced C# on June 26, 2000, as a modern, object-oriented language built for .NET that would let millions of C and C++ developers reuse their skills. It submitted the specification to ECMA at the same time, and ECMA-334 was published in December 2001. C# 1.0 shipped with Visual Studio .NET in January 2002 and looked a lot like Java.

Later versions pulled in ideas from functional programming, many by way of F#, which Microsoft Research built on .NET: generics in 2005, LINQ in 2007 and `async`/`await` in 2012. In 2014 Microsoft open-sourced its managed compilers, Roslyn among them, and announced that .NET Core, the base of a cross-platform .NET, would be open source too.

choices.choice: Stay close to C and C++
choices.why: The target audience was the huge base of C and C++ programmers. Familiar syntax let them move to .NET without learning a new notation.

choices.choice: Standardize through ECMA from the start
choices.why: Microsoft wanted other vendors to be able to implement the language, and submitted the specification to ECMA the day it announced C#.

Java’s generics, based on GJ, erase type arguments at compile time. .NET generics, designed at Microsoft Research and shipped with C# 2.0 in 2005, let the runtime JIT-compile code for each instantiation, so type information stays accurate at run time and integers need no boxing.
C# 5.0 focused almost entirely on `async` and `await`, letting the compiler turn sequential-looking code into callbacks instead of making developers write them by hand.

timeline.text: Microsoft announces C# on June 26 and submits it to ECMA
C# 1.0 ships with Visual Studio .NET in January
C# 3.0 adds LINQ and lambda expressions
Microsoft open-sources .NET Core, after its C#, VB and F# compilers
C# 14 ships in November, the sixth yearly November release
